"# Summary

The Home Assistant Companion app for Android accepts a server URL from a `homeassistant://invite` deep link and begins the onboarding flow against that server **without ever displaying the destination URL to the user**. Because the user is never shown which server they are about to connect to, a crafted invitation can silently point onboarding at an attacker-controlled server, whose login page is then loaded inside the app's onboarding WebView — which has **no URL bar and no domain indicator**. The attacker could render a pixel-perfect Home Assistant login page and harvest the victim's credentials.

# Details

The core defect is the **missing disclosure of the destination server URL**: at no point in the invitation/onboarding flow was the user shown the hostname they were about to trust, so they had no way to tell a legitimate invite from a malicious one.

The handler `io.homeassistant.companion.android.launch.link.LinkHandlerImpl.handleInviteLink(Uri)` read a server URL from the URI fragment (`#url=...`) and passed it verbatim into `LinkDestination.Onboarding`:

```kotlin
private fun handleInviteLink(uri: Uri): LinkDestination {
    var encodedFragment = uri.encodedFragment ?: ""        // "url=https://attacker.example"
    var parse: Uri? = Uri.parse("https://?$encodedFragment")
    if (parse.isOpaque) parse = null
    val url = parse?.getQueryParameter("url") ?: return LinkDestination.NoDestination
    return LinkDestination.Onboarding(url)                 // no hostname shown, no confirmation
}
```

There was no screen anywhere that displayed the parsed hostname before onboarding committed to it. Because invitations are meant to onboard brand-new users. One tap on the legitimate-looking "Connect to my Home Assistant server" button then opened the attacker's `/auth/authorize` endpoint in the onboarding WebView.

Successful credential theft gives the attacker access to the victim's Home Assistant account.

Weakness classes: [CWE-601](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/601.html) URL Redirection to Untrusted Site (Open Redirect); [CWE-451](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/451.html) User Interface (UI) Misrepresentation of Critical Information.

# Affected versions

Home Assistant Companion for Android (full `io.homeassistant.companion.android`, minimal `io.homeassistant.companion.android.minimal`, and Android Automotive): `<= 2026.5.5` (reported and verified on `2026.5.4`).

# Patched versions

`2026.6.1` (PR home-assistant/android#6955).

# Impact

**CVSS 3.1:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N` — **4.3 (Medium)**

The link can be delivered remotely (`AV:N`) and exploitation requires the user to follow the flow and enter credentials (`UI:R`). The direct technical impact is disclosure of the Home Assistant credentials the user types into the spoofed page (`C:L`).

| Impact | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **Credential theft** | The HA username and password are sent to the attacker server via the spoofed login page. |
| **Smart-home takeover** | HA credentials govern locks, cameras, alarms, garage doors, thermostats → physical-safety risk. |
| **Password reuse** | Many users reuse HA passwords across services. |
| **No on-device indicators** | The onboarding WebView has no URL bar, no domain hint, and (pre-fix) no screen displayed the destination hostname. |

_Note: the reporter's `C:L` / 4.3 reflects that the attacker obtains only what the victim types and that scope is unchanged. Given the downstream physical-safety consequences, a higher confidentiality rating is arguable, but `C:L`/4.3 is a reasonable base score._

# Steps to reproduce

Having the application installed, no root/ADB/MITM required.

1. Stand up a server that mimics the Home Assistant OAuth endpoints (`/auth/providers`, `/auth/authorize`, `/auth/login_flow/...`) and serves a look-alike login page.
2. Deliver the invite deep link to the victim through any `ACTION_VIEW` source — a web `<a href>`/redirect, a Chrome `intent://` bridge, a cross-app intent, a QR/NFC tag, or a message:
   ```
   homeassistant://invite/#url=https://attacker.example
   ```
3. The app commits onboarding to the attacker URL **without showing the hostname**. The victim taps "Connect to my Home Assistant server".
4. The onboarding WebView loads `https://attacker.example/auth/authorize…`; the spoofed page captures the credentials the victim enters.

Logcat confirms the app builds the OAuth URL against the attacker host with no validation:
```
ConnectionViewModel: Building auth url based on https://attacker.example
ConnectionViewModel: Auth url is: https://attacker.example/auth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=https://home-assistant.io/android&redirect_uri=homeassistant://auth-callback
```

# Workaround

If you cannot upgrade immediately:

- Do not open Home Assistant invitation links from untrusted sources (web pages, email, SMS, QR/NFC tags, other apps).
- Only complete onboarding/login against a server URL you recognize and trust; if a login page appears that you did not initiate against your own server, do not enter credentials.

The robust mitigation is to upgrade to a patched version.

# Fix

Update the Companion app to `2026.6.1` or later.

The fix is **transparency and explicit user review of the destination server URL** before any connection is made — the invitation flow no longer trusts a URL the user has not seen.

PR home-assistant/android#6955 routes invitations to a dedicated `WelcomeInvitationScreen` that prominently **discloses the destination server URL** and warns about the risk of accepting an invitation, so the user can see exactly which server they are about to connect to before proceeding.

# Acknowledgements
